_note: Quote of the day (/conoscenze/citazioni). Italian-language quotations only, in their traditional wording, by authors who died before 1946, which puts them in the public domain under Italy's life+70 rule (Legge 633/1941, art. 25). Every quote is a line from the author's own work and `source` names that work (with canto, chapter or poem where we are fairly sure); `year` is the year of first publication or, for the old poems, an approximate date of writing. Famously misattributed lines are left out on purpose (for example 'Il fine giustifica i mezzi', 'Eppur si muove'). Verse line breaks are ' / ' (oneLine() in zitateData.js turns them into spaces). `disputed: true` would show a badge; no quote needs it. `meaning` says the quote in plain English (A2-B1). Word fields keep their old names: `de` is the Italian word, `art` il, lo, la, l', i, gli or le (`pos` for words without an article). Spelling of old texts follows common editions; some lines were quoted from memory and are listed 'to verify' in tmp-culture/zitate-filme-kalender.verify.md. Written 2026-11-15.

dante.name: Dante Alighieri
dante.bio: Dante wrote the Divine Comedy, a long poem about a journey through Hell, Purgatory and Paradise. He wrote it in the Florentine of his time, not in Latin, and that helped to make it the base of standard Italian. He spent his last twenty years in exile from Florence.

francesco.name: Francis of Assisi
francesco.bio: Francis gave up a rich family life to live in poverty and to preach. His Canticle of the Creatures, written in the language of Umbria, is one of the oldest great poems in Italian. The Church made him a saint, and he is a patron saint of Italy.
francesco.kurz: His poem about the sun and the moon is one of the first in Italian.

lorenzo.name: Lorenzo de’ Medici
lorenzo.bio: Lorenzo, called “the Magnificent”, ruled Florence in the Renaissance. He supported artists and writers and also wrote poems and carnival songs himself.
lorenzo.kurz: He ruled Florence and wrote carnival songs.

petrarca.name: Francesco Petrarca
petrarca.bio: Petrarca is known in English as Petrarch. His Canzoniere, 366 poems mostly about a woman called Laura, shaped love poetry in Europe for centuries. He also wrote in Latin and travelled a lot.
petrarca.kurz: He wrote love poems about Laura.

boccaccio.name: Giovanni Boccaccio
boccaccio.bio: Boccaccio wrote the Decameron, a hundred stories told by ten young people who leave Florence during the plague of 1348. The stories are funny, sad and often about love and clever tricks.
boccaccio.kurz: He wrote the Decameron, a book of one hundred stories.

machiavelli.name: Niccolò Machiavelli
machiavelli.bio: Machiavelli worked for the Florentine republic and later wrote about politics. His short book Il Principe describes how rulers really behave, not how they should behave. Because of this, people still use the word “Machiavellian”.
machiavelli.kurz: He wrote Il Principe, a book about power.

ariosto.name: Ludovico Ariosto
ariosto.bio: Ariosto worked at the court of the Este family in Ferrara. His long poem Orlando furioso is full of knights, magic, love and adventure, and it was read all over Europe.
ariosto.kurz: He wrote the poem Orlando furioso.

tasso.name: Torquato Tasso
tasso.bio: Tasso wrote the Gerusalemme liberata, a poem about the First Crusade. He had a hard life with illness and long stays in hospital. Later poets and composers took many stories from his work.
tasso.kurz: He wrote the poem Gerusalemme liberata.

galileo.name: Galileo Galilei
galileo.bio: Galileo studied the sky with a telescope and showed that the Earth moves around the sun. The Church put him on trial for it. He wrote his books in Italian so that more people could read them.
galileo.kurz: He was a scientist who wrote in clear Italian.

leopardi.name: Giacomo Leopardi
leopardi.bio: Leopardi grew up in a small town in the Marche, in a house full of books, and was often ill. His short poems about nature, hope and loneliness are among the best in Italian. Many Italian pupils learn them at school.
leopardi.kurz: He wrote short, famous poems about hope and loneliness.

manzoni.name: Alessandro Manzoni
manzoni.bio: Manzoni wrote I promessi sposi (The Betrothed), the most famous Italian novel of the 19th century. He changed its language for the final edition so that it was closer to the speech of Florence, and this helped many Italians to read and write in the same Italian.
manzoni.kurz: He wrote the novel I promessi sposi.

foscolo.name: Ugo Foscolo
foscolo.bio: Foscolo was born on a Greek island that was then Venetian. He took part in the politics of his time and died in exile in England. His poem Dei Sepolcri is about memory and the graves of great people.
foscolo.kurz: A poet who lived in exile and wrote about memory.

carducci.name: Giosuè Carducci
carducci.bio: Carducci was a poet and a professor at the University of Bologna. In 1906 he was the first Italian to win the Nobel Prize in Literature.
carducci.kurz: The first Italian to win the Nobel Prize in Literature.

pascoli.name: Giovanni Pascoli
pascoli.bio: Pascoli lost his father when he was a boy, shot on the road home, and many of his poems are about family, death and the countryside. He used simple words in very careful rhythm. He was a teacher and professor.
pascoli.kurz: A poet of the countryside, of family and of sadness.

verga.name: Giovanni Verga
verga.bio: Verga came from Sicily and wrote about poor people there. In I Malavoglia, a family of fishermen loses its boat and its luck. He tried to let the village tell the story in its own voice.
verga.kurz: He wrote about poor people in Sicily.

collodi.name: Carlo Collodi
collodi.bio: Collodi is the pen name of Carlo Lorenzini, a journalist from Florence. He wrote Le avventure di Pinocchio, the story of a wooden puppet that becomes a boy. It is one of the most translated books in the world.

deamicis.name: Edmondo De Amicis
deamicis.bio: De Amicis was a writer and a former army officer. His book Cuore (“Heart”) is the diary of a schoolboy in Turin. Italian children read it for generations, and it is now seen as part of the history of the young Italian state.
deamicis.kurz: He wrote Cuore, a book about school life.

svevo.name: Italo Svevo
svevo.bio: Svevo is the pen name of Ettore Schmitz, who worked in a bank and later in a paint factory in Trieste. His novel La coscienza di Zeno is funny and is about a man who cannot stop smoking and cannot stop thinking about himself.
svevo.kurz: He wrote La coscienza di Zeno.

pirandello.name: Luigi Pirandello
pirandello.bio: Pirandello wrote about the question who we really are: one person can look different to every other person. He won the Nobel Prize in Literature in 1934. His best-known plays include Sei personaggi in cerca d’autore.
pirandello.kurz: He wrote plays and novels about identity.

deledda.name: Grazia Deledda
deledda.bio: Deledda was born on Sardinia and wrote about its people and customs. In 1926 she won the Nobel Prize in Literature, the only Italian woman to do so so far.
deledda.kurz: A Sardinian writer who won the Nobel Prize.

dannunzio.name: Gabriele D’Annunzio
dannunzio.bio: D’Annunzio was a very famous poet who also lived a loud public life as a soldier and a politician. His poems about nature are full of music. His later political role was controversial.
dannunzio.kurz: A poet whose verse sounds like music.

quotes.author: dante
quotes.text: Nel mezzo del cammin di nostra vita / mi ritrovai per una selva oscura, / ché la diritta via era smarrita.
quotes.meaning: In the middle of his life, the poet finds himself in a dark forest, because he has lost the right way.

words.hint: to lose; to lose the way

quotes.author: dante
quotes.text: Lasciate ogne speranza, voi ch'intrate.
quotes.meaning: This is written over the gate of Hell: leave every hope behind, you who go in.

words.hint: the feeling that things will be good

quotes.author: dante
quotes.text: Nessun maggior dolore / che ricordarsi del tempo felice / ne la miseria.
quotes.meaning: There is no greater pain than to remember happy times when you are in misery.

words.hint: to bring something back to mind
a state of great poverty or unhappiness

quotes.author: dante
quotes.text: Galeotto fu 'l libro e chi lo scrisse.
quotes.meaning: Francesca says that a book about love, and the man who wrote it, brought her and Paolo together. Today galeotto means someone or something that helps lovers to meet.

words.hint: someone or something that brings people together

quotes.author: dante
quotes.text: Fatti non foste a viver come bruti, / ma per seguir virtute e canoscenza.
quotes.meaning: Ulysses tells his men: you were not made to live like animals, but to follow goodness and knowledge.

quotes.author: dante
quotes.text: Capo ha cosa fatta.
quotes.meaning: A thing that is done has an end. It is said by a man who urged a murder: once it is done, it is done. Today people use it for a decision that cannot be undone.

quotes.author: dante
quotes.text: del bel paese là dove 'l sì suona
quotes.meaning: Dante means Italy, the beautiful country where people say “sì” for yes. Il Bel Paese is still a name for Italy.

quotes.author: dante
quotes.text: come sa di sale / lo pane altrui, e come è duro calle / lo scendere e 'l salir per l'altrui scale
quotes.meaning: Dante is told that the bread of other people tastes of salt and that it is hard to go up and down other people's stairs. He is speaking about life in exile.

words.hint: steps to go up and down

quotes.author: dante
quotes.text: L'amor che move il sole e l'altre stelle.
quotes.meaning: This is the last line of the Divine Comedy. Love moves the sun and the other stars.

words.hint: a strong feeling of care for someone
the star that gives us light
a bright point in the night sky

quotes.author: francesco
quotes.text: Laudato sie, mi' Signore, cum tucte le tue creature, / spetialmente messor lo frate Sole
quotes.meaning: Be praised, my Lord, with all your creatures, and above all with brother Sun. The old spelling shows the language of the early 1200s.

words.hint: the star that gives us light

quotes.author: lorenzo
quotes.text: Quant'è bella giovinezza, / che si fugge tuttavia! / Chi vuol esser lieto, sia: / di doman non c'è certezza.
quotes.meaning: How beautiful is youth, but it runs away! If you want to be happy, be happy now, because tomorrow is not certain.

quotes.author: petrarca
quotes.text: Solo et pensoso i più deserti campi / vo mesurando a passi tardi et lenti
quotes.meaning: Alone and full of thoughts, I walk through the most empty fields, with slow and tired steps.

quotes.author: petrarca
quotes.text: Pace non trovo, et non ho da far guerra; / et temo, et spero; et ardo, et son un ghiaccio
quotes.meaning: I find no peace and yet I do not fight a war. I fear and I hope, I burn and I am ice. This is how the poet describes being in love.

words.hint: a state without war or worry

quotes.author: boccaccio
quotes.text: Umana cosa è aver compassione degli afflitti.
quotes.meaning: It is a human thing to feel sorry for people who suffer. This is the first sentence of the Decameron.

quotes.author: machiavelli
quotes.text: Ognuno vede quel che tu pari, pochi sentono quel che tu sei.
quotes.meaning: Everybody sees what you seem to be, but few people feel what you really are. For a ruler, how you look matters more than how you are.

quotes.author: machiavelli
quotes.text: è meglio essere impetuoso che respettivo, perché la fortuna è donna
quotes.meaning: It is better to be bold than careful, because luck is a woman. She likes people who act with courage. The image is old and sounds strange today.

quotes.author: ariosto
quotes.text: Le donne, i cavallier, l'arme, gli amori, / le cortesie, l'audaci imprese io canto
quotes.meaning: I sing of the ladies, the knights, the arms and the loves, the acts of courtesy and the brave deeds. These are the first lines of the poem.

words.hint: a man who fights on a horse

quotes.author: tasso
quotes.text: Canto l'arme pietose e 'l capitano / che 'l gran sepolcro liberò di Cristo.
quotes.meaning: I sing of the holy arms and of the captain who freed the great tomb of Christ.

words.hint: the leader of a group of soldiers

quotes.author: galileo
quotes.text: La filosofia è scritta in questo grandissimo libro, che continuamente ci sta aperto innanzi a gli occhi (io dico l'universo), ma non si può intendere se prima non s'impara a intender la lingua
quotes.meaning: Philosophy is written in the great book that is always open in front of our eyes: the universe. But you cannot understand it before you learn its language. For Galileo that language is mathematics.

words.hint: the part of the face you see with

quotes.author: leopardi
quotes.text: Sempre caro mi fu quest'ermo colle, / e questa siepe, che da tanta parte / dell'ultimo orizzonte il guardo esclude.
quotes.meaning: This lonely hill has always been dear to me, and this hedge which hides most of the far horizon from my eyes.

words.hint: the line where sky meets earth

quotes.author: leopardi
quotes.text: Così tra questa / immensità s'annega il pensier mio: / e il naufragar m'è dolce in questo mare.
quotes.meaning: My thought drowns in this endless space, and to be lost in this sea is sweet to me. These are the last lines of the poem.

words.hint: the salt water that covers much of the earth

quotes.author: leopardi
quotes.text: Silvia, rimembri ancora / quel tempo della tua vita mortale, / quando beltà splendea / negli occhi tuoi ridenti e fuggitivi
quotes.meaning: Silvia, do you still remember the time of your mortal life, when beauty shone in your happy, quick eyes? The poet speaks to a young woman who died.

words.hint: an old word for to remember

quotes.author: leopardi
quotes.text: Che fai tu, luna, in ciel? dimmi, che fai, / silenziosa luna?
quotes.source: Canto notturno di un pastore errante dell'Asia
quotes.meaning: A shepherd asks the moon: what are you doing in the sky, silent moon?

words.hint: what shines in the sky at night

quotes.author: manzoni
quotes.text: Questo matrimonio non s'ha da fare, né domani, né mai.
quotes.meaning: Two men threaten the priest Don Abbondio: this wedding must not take place, not tomorrow and not ever. It is a famous line of the book.

quotes.author: manzoni
quotes.text: Carneade! Chi era costui?
quotes.meaning: Don Abbondio is reading and finds a name he does not know: Carneades! Who was that? Italians still say it when they have never heard of a person.

quotes.author: manzoni
quotes.text: Il coraggio, uno, se non ce l'ha, non se lo può dare.
quotes.meaning: Don Abbondio says that if you do not have courage, you cannot give it to yourself.

quotes.author: manzoni
quotes.text: Fu vera gloria? Ai posteri / l'ardua sentenza
quotes.meaning: Was it true glory? Future generations must give the hard judgment. The poem is about the death of Napoleon.

quotes.author: foscolo
quotes.text: A egregie cose il forte animo accendono / l'urne de' forti, o Pindemonte
quotes.meaning: The tombs of strong people light up a strong mind to great deeds, my friend Pindemonte.

quotes.author: foscolo
quotes.text: Né più mai toccherò le sacre sponde / ove il mio corpo fanciulletto giacque
quotes.meaning: I will never again touch the holy shores where I lay as a small child. The poet speaks about his island.

quotes.author: carducci
quotes.text: La nebbia a gl'irti colli / piovigginando sale, / e sotto il maestrale / urla e biancheggia il mar
quotes.meaning: The fog goes up the rough hills in a light rain. Under the north-west wind the sea howls and turns white. It is a poem about an autumn day.

words.hint: low cloud close to the ground

quotes.author: pascoli
quotes.text: San Lorenzo, io lo so perché tanto / di stelle per l'aria tranquilla / arde e cade, perché si gran pianto / nel concavo cielo sfavilla.
quotes.meaning: Saint Lawrence, I know why so many stars burn and fall through the quiet air, and why so many tears shine in the sky. On 10 August, the night of the shooting stars, the poet remembers his father.

words.hint: a bright point in the night sky

quotes.author: pascoli
quotes.text: Gemmea l'aria, il sole così chiaro / che tu ricerchi gli albicocchi in fiore
quotes.meaning: The air is clear like a jewel and the sun so bright that you look for apricot trees in flower. But it is November, and the poem will turn sad.

words.hint: the coloured part of a plant

quotes.author: verga
quotes.text: Un tempo i Malavoglia erano stati numerosi come i sassi della strada vecchia di Trezza
quotes.meaning: Once the Malavoglia family had been as numerous as the stones of the old road of Trezza. The book will tell how they lose everything.

quotes.author: collodi
quotes.text: C'era una volta... — Un re! — dissero subito i miei piccoli lettori. — No, ragazzi, avete sbagliato. C'era una volta un pezzo di legno.
quotes.meaning: The story begins with a joke. The little readers think: a king! But no, it was a piece of wood.

words.hint: the man who rules a kingdom
what a tree is made of

quotes.author: collodi
quotes.text: ci sono le bugie che hanno le gambe corte, e le bugie che hanno il naso lungo
quotes.meaning: The Fairy tells Pinocchio there are two kinds of lies: those with short legs, which are soon caught, and those with a long nose. “Le bugie hanno le gambe corte” is now a common saying.

words.hint: the part of the face you smell with

quotes.author: deamicis
quotes.text: Oggi primo giorno di scuola. Questi tre mesi di campagna sono passati come un sogno.
quotes.source: Cuore, October (“Il primo giorno di scuola”)
quotes.meaning: A boy writes in his diary: today is the first day of school. The three months in the country went by like a dream.

words.hint: what you see when you sleep

quotes.author: svevo
quotes.text: La vita non è né brutta né bella, ma è originale!
quotes.meaning: Life is neither ugly nor beautiful, but it is original.

quotes.author: pirandello
quotes.text: Una delle poche cose, anzi forse la sola ch'io sapessi di certo, era questa: che mi chiamavo Mattia Pascal.
quotes.meaning: One of the few things I knew for sure, or perhaps the only one, was this: that my name was Mattia Pascal. The hero will soon lose even this.

quotes.author: deledda
quotes.text: Siamo noi le canne, e la sorte è il vento.
quotes.meaning: We are the reeds, and fate is the wind. The old servant Efix says it about people who cannot choose their way.

words.hint: a tall thin plant that bends
what happens to you, luck or fate

quotes.author: dannunzio
quotes.text: Taci. Su le soglie / del bosco non odo / parole che dici / umane; ma odo / parole più nuove / che parlano gocciole e foglie / lontane.
quotes.source: La pioggia nel pineto, in Alcyone
quotes.meaning: Be quiet. At the edge of the wood I do not hear the human words you say, but new words that drops and far leaves speak.

words.hint: the green part of a tree

quotes.author: dannunzio
quotes.text: Settembre, andiamo. È tempo di migrare.
quotes.meaning: September, let's go. It is time to migrate. The shepherds of Abruzzo lead their sheep from the mountains down to the sea.

words.hint: to move to another place for the season
